Get started with jtb2026

Source: vignettes/jtb2026.Rmd
jtb2026.Rmd

Find the rows of a table that mention what you are looking for.

jtb2026 does one thing: you hand it a table and a word, and it hands back the rows that mention it. The table can be an Excel workbook, a CSV, or a data frame you already have; the answer can be returned to R, written to a CSV, or both.

There are two ways to ask the question, and the difference between them is the whole point of the package:

jtb_search_keyword() jtb_search_semantic()
Asks Does this row contain the word? How close is this row to the idea?
Returns Every match, in the original row order The best matches, ranked, with a score
Finds "nauseous" when you search "stomach upset" No Yes
Reproducible, offline, no model Yes Yes

Each has a vignette of its own: vignette("keyword-search"), vignette("semantic-search") and vignette("files-and-output").

Install 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("yh202109/jtb2026", build_vignettes = TRUE)
library(jtb2026)

The mock table

The package ships site_reports, twenty-four invented rows of study-site comments. Everything in these vignettes is computed against it. The comment column is the interesting one — it is free text, written by different people who described the same things in different words.

str(site_reports)
#> 'data.frame':    24 obs. of  9 variables:
#>  $ report_id  : chr  "R001" "R002" "R003" "R004" ...
#>  $ site       : chr  "Boston" "Boston" "Boston" "Boston" ...
#>  $ subject    : chr  "S-1001" "S-1002" "S-1003" "S-1004" ...
#>  $ visit      : chr  "Week 2" "Week 2" "Week 4" "Week 8" ...
#>  $ term       : chr  "Headache" "Nausea" "Fatigue" "Rash" ...
#>  $ comment    : chr  "Subject reported a dull headache starting two hours after the morning dose; resolved without treatment." "Subject felt queasy through the afternoon and skipped the evening meal." "Reported feeling unusually tired all week and needing an extra nap each day." "Small itchy patch on the left forearm, no spreading noted at review." ...
#>  $ severity   : chr  "Mild" "Moderate" "Mild" "Mild" ...
#>  $ outcome    : chr  "Recovered" "Recovered" "Ongoing" "Recovered" ...
#>  $ report_date: Date, format: "2026-01-06" "2026-01-07" "2026-01-21" ...
head(site_reports[, c("report_id", "site", "term", "comment")], 5)
report_id site term comment
R001 Boston Headache Subject reported a dull headache starting two hours after the morning dose; resolved without treatment.
R002 Boston Nausea Subject felt queasy through the afternoon and skipped the evening meal.
R003 Boston Fatigue Reported feeling unusually tired all week and needing an extra nap each day.
R004 Boston Rash Small itchy patch on the left forearm, no spreading noted at review.
R005 Denver Headache Persistent head pain over three days, described as pressure behind the eyes.

Sixty-second tour

Find rows containing a word 

hits <- jtb_search_keyword(site_reports, "headache",
                           columns = c("term", "comment"))
hits[, c("report_id", "term", "comment")]
report_id term comment
1 R001 Headache Subject reported a dull headache starting two hours after the morning dose; resolved without treatment.
5 R005 Headache Persistent head pain over three days, described as pressure behind the eyes.
14 R014 Headache Mild headche noted in the diary, no medication taken.
21 R021 Headache Sharp pain across the forehead, subject took paracetamol with relief.

Four rows, in the order they appear in the table. Note the row names — 1, 5, 14, 21 — they are the positions in the input, so you can always trace a result back.

Find rows that mean something

Nobody in this table wrote “stomach upset”. The keyword search says so:

nrow(jtb_search_keyword(site_reports, "stomach upset", columns = "comment"))
#> [1] 0

The semantic search finds all four nausea rows anyway, ranked:

ranked <- jtb_search_semantic(site_reports, "stomach upset",
                              columns = "comment", top_n = 4)
ranked[, c("report_id", "term", "comment", ".score")]
report_id term comment .score
9 R009 Nausea Stomach felt unsettled after each dose and the subject vomited once on Day 9. 0.533332
24 R024 Nausea Reported feeling sick to the stomach for an hour after dosing. 0.403267
17 R017 Nausea Nauseous most mornings this cycle, improving by midday. 0.129933
2 R002 Nausea Subject felt queasy through the afternoon and skipped the evening meal. 0.115708

R009 mentions the stomach directly and scores highest. R002 only says “queasy” and scores lowest. The ordering is the useful part: it is a ranking, not a yes/no.

Write the answer to a CSV

Both functions take output_csv. The file gets exactly what the function returns.

out <- file.path(tempdir(), "headache_rows.csv")

hits <- jtb_search_keyword(site_reports, "headache", output_csv = out)

nrow(hits)
#> [1] 4
readLines(out, n = 2)
#> [1] "\"report_id\",\"site\",\"subject\",\"visit\",\"term\",\"comment\",\"severity\",\"outcome\",\"report_date\""                                                                                          
#> [2] "\"R001\",\"Boston\",\"S-1001\",\"Week 2\",\"Headache\",\"Subject reported a dull headache starting two hours after the morning dose; resolved without treatment.\",\"Mild\",\"Recovered\",2026-01-06"

Which columns get searched

Both functions take columns, and it accepts three shapes. All three of these search the same two columns:

by_name <- jtb_search_keyword(site_reports, "Nausea",
                              columns = c("term", "comment"))
by_position <- jtb_search_keyword(site_reports, "Nausea", columns = c(5, 6))

mask <- names(site_reports) %in% c("term", "comment")
by_mask <- jtb_search_keyword(site_reports, "Nausea", columns = mask)

identical(by_name, by_position)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(by_name, by_mask)
#> [1] TRUE

Positions are 1-based and refer to the columns of the table as read, so columns = c(5, 6) is the fifth and sixth column. Leaving columns out searches everything — convenient, but it means an identifier column can match by accident:

# "R002" is a report id, not a comment; searching every column finds it.
jtb_search_keyword(site_reports, "R002")[, c("report_id", "term")]
report_id term
2 R002 Nausea

Which one should you use?

Reach for jtb_search_keyword() when you know the exact string — a subject id, a coded term, a site name — and you need every row that contains it. It is exhaustive and its answer does not depend on any tuning.

Reach for jtb_search_semantic() when you are searching free text for an idea and you do not know how the writer phrased it. It returns a ranked shortlist, so treat it as triage: read the top of the list, not the whole thing.

A practical pattern is to use both. Rank first to find the vocabulary people actually used, then keyword-search that vocabulary to get the complete set:

shortlist <- jtb_search_semantic(site_reports, "stomach upset",
                                 columns = "comment", top_n = 5)
shortlist$comment
#> [1] "Stomach felt unsettled after each dose and the subject vomited once on Day 9."
#> [2] "Reported feeling sick to the stomach for an hour after dosing."               
#> [3] "Nauseous most mornings this cycle, improving by midday."                      
#> [4] "Subject felt queasy through the afternoon and skipped the evening meal."

# Having read those, the words worth an exhaustive search are clear.
complete <- jtb_search_keyword(site_reports,
                               c("queasy", "nauseous", "stomach", "vomited"),
                               columns = "comment")
complete[, c("report_id", "comment")]
report_id comment
2 R002 Subject felt queasy through the afternoon and skipped the evening meal.
9 R009 Stomach felt unsettled after each dose and the subject vomited once on Day 9.
17 R017 Nauseous most mornings this cycle, improving by midday.
24 R024 Reported feeling sick to the stomach for an hour after dosing.
